title: Pay and recordkeeping fundamentals
audience: Any owner or office worker who records hours, pay and supporting documents for people engaged in any service business.
learningOutcomes: Describe the records a business keeps about the hours, pay and entitlements of people it engages.
Explain why accurate time records support pay, safety and dispute resolution.
Identify where the pay rules must be checked, rather than relying on this lesson for them.

instruction.heading: Why records matter
instruction.body: Records of hours, pay, leave and engagement are both a legal requirement for employers and a practical tool. They show that people were paid correctly, they support the business if a payment is questioned, and they help the business plan rosters and job times. The records should be accurate, complete and made at the time the work is done, not reconstructed later from memory.

instruction.heading: What to record
instruction.body: For each person engaged, record the start and end time of each shift, the breaks, the jobs and sites worked, any allowance or expense claimed, and the pay rate that applies. For a contractor, record the invoice, the agreed rate and the date paid. Keep signed or approved timesheets, and keep payslips or payment records where they are required. Do not record a time that was not worked, and do not alter a record without a dated note.

instruction.heading: Where pay rules come from
instruction.body: Pay rates, penalty rates, allowances, superannuation, leave and the record-keeping rules are set by national and state law and by any applicable award or agreement. These rules change and vary by industry and by the person's classification. This lesson does not state any pay rate, penalty or entitlement, because none is confirmed here. Check the current rules with the Fair Work Ombudsman, the relevant state authority or a qualified adviser before setting any pay.

procedure: Record the start, finish, breaks, jobs and sites for each person's shift at the time.
Record any allowance or expense claimed, with supporting documents.
Keep approved timesheets and invoices in the approved system.
Correct any error with a dated note, not by altering the original.
Check the pay rules with the relevant authority or adviser before setting pay.
Keep records for the period the law requires, and review the retention rule periodically.

workedExamples.situation: A worker's timesheet shows a shift that ended earlier than the job log shows, and the worker asks you to change the timesheet to match the lower figure.
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not change the record to suit either side without evidence. Compare the timesheet with the job log and any other evidence, check the pay rule with the relevant authority or adviser, and record the discrepancy with a dated note. Resolve it with the worker before the pay run.

commonErrors.error: Reconstructing timesheets from memory at the end of the week.
commonErrors.prevention: Record times at the time the work is done.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Employers have record-keeping and pay obligations under national and state law and under any applicable award or agreement.

qualityStandard: Each shift has a time record made at the time of work.
Each correction is dated and traceable.
No pay rate is set without a confirmed source.
documentationEvidence: Timesheet and job log for each shift.
Invoice and payment records for each contractor.
summary: Record hours and jobs at the time, and correct only with dated notes.
Keep pay, invoice and expense records in the approved system.
Check the current pay rules with the relevant authority before setting pay.

knowledgeChecks.question: How should a timesheet error be corrected?
options: Add a dated note and keep the original visible.
Ask the worker to change it without a record.

knowledgeChecks.question: Where should the current pay rules be checked?
options: In a colleague's memory and the notes from last year and the staff rota.
With the Fair Work Ombudsman, the relevant state authority or a qualified adviser.
On a pay site and a forum for workers in the city and on a social media post.

knowledgeChecks.question: When should work records be made, according to the lesson?
options: Only when a payment is questioned
Once a year, at tax time
At the time the work is done
